topic_candidates.title: How AI Is Starting to Rewrite Itself
topic_candidates.query: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights arXiv 2611.21885
topic_candidates.brief: Explain a new experiment in which a language model edits parts of its own internal weights, tests the result, and becomes better without ordinary gradient training. Start with the simple idea of changing a model’s stored connections, then show the loop: inspect, edit, test, keep or discard. The viewer should understand why this is not yet a self-aware AI, but could make future models cheaper to adapt and harder to audit. The science angle is weight-space optimization and generalization to unseen problems.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: The researchers report that a model rewrote its own weights using its reasoning process, without gradients or additional training, and improved by 6.6 percentage points on a fixed set of previously unseen problems. This is an early research result, not evidence that commercial chatbots can freely redesign themselves. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21885?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: November 18, 2026 — the paper was published five days before the current brief.
topic_candidates.science_angle: Neural-network weights, self-directed optimization, test-set generalization, and why changing parameters is different from retraining a model from scratch.

topic_candidates.title: The AI-Designed CPU That Could Change Chips
topic_candidates.query: Frostbite AI-designed CPU architecture Architect Labs November 2026
topic_candidates.brief: Explain how Frostbite’s developers used AI across the entire chip-design loop: proposing an instruction set, building a processor model, generating a design, and checking that the implementation obeys its specification. The story should make clear what AI actually did and what humans still had to define and verify. Ordinary viewers leave understanding why chip design is slow, why verification is the bottleneck, and why an AI-generated architecture matters even before it reaches phones or laptops. The engineering underneath is instruction-set architecture, formal contracts, hardware synthesis, and verification.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: Architect Labs says Frostbite was discovered, designed, and verified end-to-end with AI, with the instruction set, model, design, and verification iterated together around a formal contract. Treat performance and production claims as claims from the company until independent benchmarks or silicon are available. ([architectlabs.com](https://architectlabs.com/blog/frostbite?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: November 18, 2026 — Architect Labs announced Frostbite four days before the current brief.
topic_candidates.science_angle: CPU instruction sets, hardware design automation, formal verification, and the difference between a verified design and a manufactured chip.

topic_candidates.title: How Claude Helped Attack a 167-Year-Old Math Problem
topic_candidates.query: Levent Alpöge Claude claimed proof Riemann hypothesis Lean November 20 2026
topic_candidates.brief: Explain the reported Claude-assisted attempt to prove the Riemann Hypothesis without presenting the claim as settled fact. Begin with why prime numbers create a hidden pattern, then show how a proof assistant such as Lean can check millions of formal steps. The key question is not simply whether an AI ‘solved math,’ but whether the formal statement, imported lemmas, and proof pipeline have all been independently checked and understood. This gives viewers a useful way to separate a dramatic AI claim from verified mathematics.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: Levent Alpöge announced on November 20, 2026 that he and Claude had developed a formalized proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Lean-community and mathematical sources describe the formalization, but the claim should remain labeled a claimed proof while independent experts validate the mathematics and its dependencies. ([leanprover-community.github.io](https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: November 20, 2026 — the claim became a major discussion topic in mathematics and AI communities.
topic_candidates.science_angle: Prime-number distribution, proof assistants, formal verification, and why machine-checked code does not automatically make a new mathematical argument easy for humans to understand.
